title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Criminals have used generative AI to create deepfakes that impersonate real people, including a South Florida immigration attorney whose voice was cloned to solicit money from immigrants. The scammers obtained personal information and voice samples from social media to make the impersonations convincing. This is a failure of impersonation, where AI systems generated false identities deployed directly to victims without human intermediation.

The impersonations succeeded because they exploited the gap between how victims verify identity and how easily AI can now replicate voice and appearance. Banks and law enforcement report that these scams are becoming harder to detect by conventional means. A code word system with family members or direct verification through known contact numbers would have prevented at least some losses, but these defenses require coordination before a scam attempt occurs.

It is not established whether the deepfake systems were built or adapted specifically for fraud, or whether criminals simply repurposed general-purpose tools.

summary:
Criminals are increasingly using artificial intelligence technology to create convincing deepfakes for scams across Georgia and South Florida. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans lost nearly $893 million to AI-enabled scams last year. Specific cases include a South Florida immigration attorney whose voice and identity were cloned to target immigrants, and a Cobb County couple who lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. Florida reported 350 AI-related complaints with nearly $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia had 71 complaints totaling more than $10.4 million in losses.

Scammers use generative AI to clone voices from social media videos, spoof phone numbers, create fake photographs, and research personal information to make emergency requests seem authentic. Common schemes include grandparent scams using voice cloning and romance scams, which caused over $19 million in losses nationwide. Banks warn that these impersonation attempts are becoming harder to detect. Authorities recommend establishing code words with family members, verifying urgent requests by contacting people directly through known numbers, and never sending money based solely on phone calls. Victims should report suspected scams to law enforcement and the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center.
